title: Visual Search Laboratory
scopeNote: This keeps the performed searches at three set sizes in both conditions, and the two search functions they produce. Target-absent trials, and the second teaching job about the ratio of absent to present slopes, are the largest cut and the page says so. The untimed inspection stage, the feedback-on-everything practice mode and the transfer challenge stay in the longer version.
summary: Find a target defined by one feature, then one defined by two features in combination, at eight, sixteen and thirty-two items. The learner's own reaction times are fitted to produce two search functions, and the number that matters is the slope rather than the speed.
learningObjectives: Define feature and conjunction search in terms of how the target is specified relative to the distractors.
Read a search function and state its slope in milliseconds per item.
Explain why the slope rather than the mean reaction time is the quantity of interest.
Distinguish a description of a search function from a mechanistic claim about parallel or serial processing.
Recognise how few trials per cell a classroom block provides, and what that does to a slope estimate.
interactionTypes: six untimed practice trials with feedback after each
a performed search block of 48 trials at three set sizes in two conditions
a keyboard or button response naming which half the target was in
least-squares search functions fitted to the learner's own means
a full table of every cell behind the chart
privacy: Nothing is collected, stored or transmitted. Every reaction time is measured and analysed in the browser and is gone when the page is closed.
accessibilityNotes: Keyboard operable throughout, with arrow keys or two labelled buttons that name the key they duplicate. No trial is ever timed out. The defining feature in the single-feature condition is orientation rather than colour, so that condition works without colour vision; the conjunction condition necessarily needs a second dimension and uses gold against blue, the colour axis that survives the common forms of colour blindness. The display description names what the target is on every trial and which half it is in, so the task can be followed without seeing the bars. The two search functions differ by marker shape and line dash as well as by colour, and are named in a key carrying a sample of each. The chart carries a description giving every mean and both slopes, and all values appear again in a table. Nothing fades, moves or animates.
dataStatus: The learner's own reaction times, produced in the moment. Nothing is a norm and nothing is compared with anyone else.
simulationNotes: Displays are generated from a seeded grid of jittered slots with a gap down the middle, so which half an item is in is never ambiguous. In the single-feature condition every bar is gold and exactly one is tilted. In the conjunction condition the target is gold and tilted, and the distractors are alternately gold and upright or blue and tilted, so every distractor shares exactly one of the target's two features and neither feature alone identifies it. Because every display contains a target, the response is which half rather than present or absent: this keeps a two-key response, makes guessing visible as an error rate, and requires the target actually to be located. Responses under 200 ms or over 12 seconds are counted, reported and kept out of the means. Slopes are ordinary least squares of the three cell means on set size.
readmeTopic: why the slope of a search function matters more than how fast anyone was
